Scientists are increasingly concerned about links to premature births and stillbirths, while outdoor workers, children and older people face particular risks. Joy Shumake-Guillemot, of WMO, explained to UN News how meteorologists and health professionals are working together to reduce some of those risks. Through a joint initiative with WHO, climate information is being brought into public health planning. A forecast of dangerously high temperatures, for example, can help hospitals prepare for more patients, while rainfall and seasonal predictions can help health authorities anticipate outbreaks of diseases such as malaria. The main character at the center of this story is not the atmosphere. It’s not the land, the ocean or the ice. It’s us – Alan Dangour, Wellcome Trust Foundation “The weather information is very practical, it is directly relevant to the decisions being made in the health sector, but they often don't have access to it,” she said. And the potential is enormous: “From a public health perspective, almost all heat deaths are actually preventable,” Ms. Shumake-Guillemot said. Health is one of the 10 priority areas of COP31’s Action Agenda, and countries are being urged to put into practice the Belém Health Action Plan agreed at COP30. A new Antalya Initiative for Health Resilience is also being launched. Agriculture: From emissions to solutions Food and agriculture account for roughly one third of global greenhouse gas emissions. But the sector is also highly vulnerable to climate change, as rising temperatures, droughts and floods threaten crops and the livelihoods of millions of farmers. Agriculture can also be part of the solution. Cristian Barrazueta, from the World Rural Forum, told UN News that farmers are already putting some of these approaches into practice. In Fiji, for example, families are experimenting with different crop varieties and finding ways to protect their seedlings from increasingly powerful cyclones. Their role is also being discussed at COP31, where countries are reviewing the Sharm el-Sheikh programme on agriculture and food security ( COP27 ) and deciding what comes next. For Mr. Barrasueta, the priority is ensuring that family farmers have a say in shaping climate policies and can access the funding needed to adapt. Conference coverage By Laura Quinones 9 November 2026 Climate and Environment Nearly 200 countries have arrived on Türkiye's Mediterranean coast for a climate summit with a different ambition: fewer grand declarations and more concrete decisions. With a powerful El Niño threatening to worsen extreme weather, negotiators face difficult questions over climate finance, clean energy and how to protect communities already living with the consequences of climate change. Today at COP31 COP31 opens: More than 90,000 people are expected in Antalya as pressure mounts to deliver on climate promises. The summit is set to close on Friday, 20 November. Australia seeks early deal: Countries are being asked to start shaping a political agreement from the outset, rather than waiting until the final days. Finance remains a sticking point: Developing countries are pressing for faster access to climate finance, while clean energy, adaptation and a just transition top the agenda. Focus on human impacts: Food, Agriculture and Health Day spotlights growing risks and practical solutions. The Mediterranean city of Antalya is no stranger to history. Greeks, Romans, Byzantines and Ottomans have all left their mark on this stretch of Türkiye’s southern coast. Now, as nearly 200 countries gather here for the latest UN climate summit, COP31 , the question is whether they can add a new chapter of their own by turning decades of climate promises into action. Inside the vast conference venue, the Turkish tulip featured in the COP31 logo is a recurring sight as participants navigate long corridors leading to national pavilions and negotiating rooms. Beyond the bustle of the conference halls, the stakes are high. The Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health (ATACH) supports countries and partners through field-tested strategies and global expertise, and the Belém Health Action Plan (BHAP) sets the priority areas for health adaptation. Regional commitments and initiatives reinforce global commitments, and Antalya is an opportunity to activate plans into action, such as through the Antalya Initiative for Health Resilience (AIR). Ask: Countries to renew and report commitments through ATACH at Antalya; implement the Belém Health Action Plan and report progress at the ministerial roundtable; reflect health in national climate and health planning, with a sustainable, prepared workforce, climate-informed health surveillance, applying a One Health approach to interventions, disaster risk reduction and emergency preparedness. Build sustained operational partnerships between health and meteorological institutions to monitor delivery. 4 B1 From Belém to Antalya, implement the Belém Health Action Plan Key message: Every COP since Glasgow has added tools, plans and policies that take action for health in the context of climate change. Action requires sound scientific, digital and technological systems to track progress, inform decisions and demonstrate results. Background • The Presidency has placed digital health and AI at the centre of the Health Day, including at ministerial level. • Countries are increasingly investing in climateinformed surveillance, air quality monitoring, climate services for health, forecasting and early warning systems and related digital capabilities. Implementation gaps remain: fragmentation between climate, meteorological and health information systems; weak governance for operational collaboration; limited experience with end-to-end systems and shared standards; no mechanism to align investments along the pathway; and wide variation in country readiness and digital maturity. • Many commitments now exist through the BHAP, ATACH and national processes, but monitoring frameworks are often weaker than commitment frameworks, limiting accountability and learning. The Global Goal on Adaptation is driving demand for measurable indicators and reporting. The ask • Countries and organisations to recognise data and digital connectivity as a foundational enabler of climate-resilient health systems, and to move from project-based coordination to sustained operational partnerships between health and meteorological institutions, so that health systems can shift from reactive to anticipatory action across extreme heat, air-quality monitoring, climatesensitive infectious diseases, early warning and emergency preparedness. • Countries and partners to connect investments across the whole pathway, building on national digital health systems with country-owned capabilities and long-term sustainability as core objectives. • Countries and organisations to ensure responsible use of technological systems, geospatial technologies and AI for climate risk assessment, surveillance, forecasting and decision-making, with safeguards for data governance, data sovereignty, equity, accuracy, transparency and environmental sustainability. • Countries to strengthen monitoring of climatehealth commitments and outcomes, contributing to reporting under the Global Goal on Adaptation, the BHAP, the WHO Global Action Plan and GPW14, and to use monitoring data to identify implementation bottlenecks and share lessons. Polluted air knows no borders, so cooperation between nations and sectors on legislation, financing and delivery saves lives and reduces warming. • Where emissions are not yet controlled at source, reducing personal exposure is an interim measure, not a substitute. This includes noncombustion particulate matter such as sand and dust storms, which land and water management can mitigate. • WHO has commissioned a systematic review and meta-analysis on the health effects of black carbon in ambient and household air pollution: full report in 2027, with a snapshot at COP31. • WHO estimates that global scale up of fiscal policies to efficiently price fossil fuels could save 1.2 million lives per year, avert 16.4 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent emissions, and generate economic welfare benefits of US$ 3.0 trillion plus fiscal benefits of US$ 5.4 trillion. The ask • Parties to include health in negotiated outcomes and BTRs, to develop clear pathways for including health in Loss and Damage mechanisms, to support health indicators under the Global Goal on Adaptation, and to consider the inclusion of health in the UNFCCC process. 10 C5 Follow the science and counter the climate infodemic, mis- and disinformation, and conflicts of interest Key message: Accurate information and scientific evidence are a precondition for climate, clean air and health action: misand disinformation, and the conflicts of interest that drive them, delay the policies that protect health. Background • There is a growing movement in the health community toward countering fossil fuel mis- and disinformation, including WHO action on mis/ disinformation and its impact on health. The ask • Governments and organisations including the media to establish a clear process for countering mis- and disinformation about climate change, air pollution and health. • Governments and partners to build the capacity of health workers and communicators to be trusted messengers, including through the wider work of WHO and by backing the Global Initiative for Information Integrity on Climate Change. 11 2. Health at COP31 2.1 The COP31 Action Agenda The COP31 President-Designate Murat Kurum set out in his third letter to the Parties an Action Agenda of ten priority themes anchored in the six axes of the Global Climate Action Agenda. Finance, technology and capacity building are cross-cutting enabling themes. Theme 8, Dynamic and Resilient Health Systems, prioritises climate-resilient and equitable health systems that can anticipate, respond to and recover from climate-related shocks, through preparedness, surveillance, resilient health infrastructure and equitable access to care. Unlike many other themes, health carries no numerical target for 2035. “ Dynamic and Resilient Health Systems focuses on developing climate-resilient and equitable health systems that can respond effectively to climate-related shocks. Rising temperatures, deteriorating air quality, changing disease patterns and more frequent extreme weather events are placing growing pressure on health systems worldwide. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), climate change could cause hundreds of thousands of additional deaths annually between 2030 and 2050 from malnutrition, malaria, diarrheal disease and heat stress alone. Against this scientific backdrop, developing climate-resilient and equitable health systems represents a science-based implementation priority. Strengthening preparedness, surveillance, resilient health infrastructure and equitable access to healthcare can reduce climate-related health risks while improving the capacity of health systems to anticipate, respond to and recover from future climate impacts. Investing in health resilience therefore delivers significant social, economic and development benefits alongside improved climate adaptation.” - President-Designate Murat Kurum in his third letter to the Parties 12 2.2 Health Day and the Antalya Initiative for Health Resilience (AIR) The dedicated Health Day at COP31 on 9 November (Day 1) is part of the Food, Agriculture and Health thematic day. The day is built around three pillars: climate-resilient health systems; connectivity and coordination; and accelerating action. It includes four high-level panels (resilient health systems; climate action and digital health; health technologies and access; humanitarian aid and health integration) and a ministerial roundtable for health ministers to forge commitments and align national priorities. The Antalya Initiative for Health Resilience (AIR “accelerating climate-health action: moving from commitment to implementation”) is a voluntary, country-driven, non-binding mechanism for sharing national experience in climate-health action, designed to enable peer learning and to bridge to COP32 and beyond. It will be inaugurated with a document setting out Türkiye’s achievements, as the standard for country contributions, and offers a non-binding, trust-based framework for sharing lessons, and a bridge to COP32 and beyond through a collective experience pool. 2.3 Key moments pre- and post-COP October 2026 WHO launches: • Priority indicators to monitor the impact of heat exposure on maternal, newborn and child health. • Technical report on the global benefits and costs of six prioritised climate– health actions. It will bring together governments, UN bodies, civil society, academia and the private sector to accelerate climate action, focusing on implementation, finance and a just transition, with an overall vision of "Dialogue. Consensus. Action." At COP31, WHO will work with partners to help place health at the heart of climate discussions by advancing climate-resilient and environmentally sustainable health systems. Building on the momentum from recent COPs, COP31 offers an opportunity to accelerate implementation, strengthen accountability and elevate country action. The vital inclusion of Dynamic and Resilient Health Systems in the COP31 Presidency’s ten priority themes signals growing recognition that health is both a frontline impact of climate change and a foundation for effective climate response. Resilient health systems help countries anticipate, prevent and respond to climate-related health risks while advancing equity, continuity of care and long-term social resilience. COP31 Health Day The dedicated COP31 Health Day will take place on the first day of the Conference, 9 November, coinciding with the thematic priorities on Food and Agriculture. The official programme of the Health Day will include four high-level panels (taking place in Special Event Room 4 - Perge Hall, Blue Zone) followed by a Ministerial convening (taking place in Special Event Room 2 - Likya Hall, Blue Zone): 10:00-11:00 - Panel 1 New Dimensions in Health: Climate-Sensitive Health Technologies and Access; 11:00-12:00 - Panel 2 Strong Climate Action and Digital Health; 12:00-13:00 - Panel 3 Humanitarian Aid and Health: Integration in Crisis Management ; 13:00-14:00 - Panel 4 Country Experiences in Building Dynamic and Resilient Health Systems ; 15:00-18:30 - Ministerial Roundtable: a dedicated space for health ministers to forge commitments and align national priorities. Other key climate-health events at COP31 include : - Baku COP Presidencies Coalition for Climate and Health High-level Roundtable on Advancing Health in the Global Climate Agenda 9 November, 18:30 19:30, Special Event Room 1. This high-level roundtable will bring together current and former COP Presidencies to take stock of progress on climate and health, strengthen political leadership and continuity across COP cycles, and identify priorities for accelerating implementation of climate and health commitments towards COP32 and beyond. - ATACH Day - 10 November, Health Pavilion, more details available here . - UN High-level Side Event " Resilient and dynamic health systems: progress from recent COPs " led by WHO in collaboration with other UN partners: UNU, UNICEF, UNDP, OHCHR, UNFPA 14 November, 15:00-16:30, Side event room 5. Health is gaining momentum within global climate agenda. This event will highlight progress from recent COPs, showcase national experiences, and explore priorities for advancing resilient and dynamic health systems through stronger climate and health action. Access the list of climate-health events at COP31 COP31 Health Pavilion The COP31 Health Pavilion will be hosting over 60 events during the two weeks of COP. Access the full programme and the live streaming COP31 priorities and key messages on climate change and health WHO’s priorities and key messages for COP31 are set out in the climate and health briefing and key messages . These outline key priorities, context and simple asks for three key areas: that climate change is causing measurable and unequal harm to health, that health systems must become climate-resilient, low-carbon and sustainable, and that health is the strongest argument for climate action, with co-benefits from cutting emissions, adapting with health in mind, financing what works and putting health in the negotiated text. More details will be made available on this webpage soon. Pre-COP activities In the run up to COP31, there is a number of activities planned to emphasize the importance of health within the climate agenda: Side Event at SB64 - 15 June 2026, Bonn, Germany As part of the lead-up to COP31, WHO, UNU, Save the Children, and the Ministry of Health of Brazil co-hosted a side event at the 64th UNFCCC Subsidiary Bodies (SB64) in Bonn. around: traffic or unable to board the few buses, shuttles and trams to the venue, fared far worse. For those brave enough to make it inside, the national pavilion halls play out like a world’s fair. Tajikistan’s is adorned with glaciers, a reminder of the Himalayan glacier collapse accelerated by climate change that killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal in August. Brazil’s is a rainforest, Oman’s a desert. Across the hall, the UK pavilion honours the man who has arguably done more than anyone to protect the ecosystems the pavilions celebrate, the 100-year-old Sir David Attenborough. UK Pavilion at COP31. From the moment planes land to when buses and trams pull into the Expo Centre grounds, COP31-themed slogans blanket the city. Some play on time (“Protecting tomorrow is today’s work”), others on public transit (“Next stop: a better future,” painted on the COP31 tram). Some are classic UN jargon (“Dialogue. Consensus. Action.”), while others are just silly (“Let’s COP!”). Yet one in particular best captures what the hosts, delegates, civil society and attendees in Antalya hope the summit will deliver: “Where dialogue becomes action.” “COP31 must help close the gap between commitment and delivery,” said Australian climate minister Chris Bowen, who presides over the negotiations under a power-sharing deal with Türkiye. He has made finance, electrification and the ocean his priorities, and advocates: “We must turn climate ambition into real-world outcomes.” So can the world deliver? “The success of the next two weeks of talks will be judged by two things. The appetite to deliver on the promises we have made, and the ability to move beyond the culture of declarations that has sullied previous conferences," said Mohamed Adow, director of the Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa. Let’s COP! A large animated dome sitting atop the food court flips through animations of the globe, COP31 logos and the Turkish flag. In hallowed COP tradition, the opening ceremony began an hour and a half late. The talks ran into Sunday night, stumbling over developing countries’ demands to put climate finance on the official agenda. Still, by previous years’ standards, this was a relatively short stalemate. While the overtime talks secured an agenda item on climate finance, a two-year work programme agreed in Belém on how rich countries meet their obligation under the Paris Agreement to fund climate action in developing ones, it came at a compromise. An African Group request for a separate item on tripling adaptation finance, the money that helps countries cope with heat, floods and failed harvests, was withdrawn after late-night talks and will be taken up under other items instead, according to Climate Home News and AFP . Adaptation finance was a key target of civil society and developing nations alike in the run-up to COP31 because of the confusion in the text agreed last year. At COP30 in Belém, countries pledged to “at least triple” adaptation finance by 2035, but never agreed on a baseline year to triple from, or a dollar figure. As it stands, depending on how it is measured, the pledge would cover just 20% to 29% of the roughly $420 billion a year, adjusted for inflation, that developing countries will need by 2035 to adapt to a fast-accelerating climate crisis, UNEP found in its annual Adaptation Gap Report last week. An interactive map charting the flight paths and emissions of COP attendees. As money continues to fall short and warming accelerates, the 44 least developed countries (LDCs) called the looming overshoot of 1.5°C “a grave betrayal of our countries who have contributed least to this crisis” in their opening-day statement. “COP31 cannot be another exercise in deferring difficult decisions,” said the group’s chair, Ambassador Adão Soares Barbosa of Timor-Leste. “It must deliver urgent emissions reductions, address temperature overshoot, access finance and tangible protection for those most at risk.” ‘Pandemic proportions’ Top health and climate officials gather at a high-level ministerial meeting on COP31’s Health Day. Türkiye opened COP31 with a Health Day, and health ministers and global health leaders from Geneva to the Pacific came to Antalya to argue that the health consequences of climate change have reached catastrophic proportions. “No health system can be made resilient to an endlessly warming world,” Simon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, told health ministers. “We must drive the transition away from fossil fuels fast and fairly.” Stiell added that a health system can falter by degree: “A ward grows hotter. The power flickers. A refrigerator holding medicines fails. Floodwater enters a well. A mother in labor finds the road to the clinic cut off.” At a separate press briefing on Monday, Stiell said the climate crisis is now “a global health crisis of pandemic proportions.” Heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths in 2023, almost three-quarters of them caused by climate change, the Lancet Countdown found last month. Air pollution from burning fossil fuels killed another 2.78 million people that year, and The Lancet authors argued that WHO should create a new category of public health emergency to classify the climate crisis. “We can say that most heat deaths around the world are caused by climate change,” said Diarmid Campbell-Lendrum, who leads WHO’s climate and health work. “They’re climate change deaths.” Money for war and death Opening plenary of COP31 in session. But as dire warnings of health threats echoed around the room, for a third consecutive COP, following Brazil and Baku, governments did not announce any new investment or financing. “Let me be direct,” said Brazil’s Health Minister, Alexandre Padilha. “Financing for health adaptation is insufficient and is falling down.” International public commitments for health adaptation fell from about $3.2 billion in 2022 to $2.2 billion in 2024, just 5% of all international public adaptation finance, Padilha said. Development aid fell 23% in 2025, its largest drop on record, according to OECD figures he cited, while global military spending has risen 41% in a decade to $2.9 trillion. “Why [is there] always so much money for war and death,” he asked, “and so little for health, environment, and life?” ‘Declarations do not protect people’ Bridge to COP31 stretches over a highway, with Antalya’s surrounding mountains in the backdrop. Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, at his last COP as WHO Director-General before his term ends next August, traced health’s climb up the climate agenda, from pledges on climate-resilient health systems in Glasgow in 2021 to the first COP Health Day in Dubai and the Belém Health Action Plan last year. “Each of those steps was driven by health ministers, but declarations do not protect people,” he said. “Implementation does.” Tuvalu Health Minister Tuafafa Latasi said he spoke “from the front line of an immediate clinical and public health emergency,” with three of his country’s nine islands at high risk from cyclones, rising seas and salt seeping into groundwater. “Protecting health in Tuvalu is a test of our shared humanity,” he said. “Our call at COP31 is simple: match strong climate commitment with practical support.” In a WHO survey last year, more than 90% of countries named insufficient finance as a top barrier to their health and climate plans, Tedros said. Yet health has no item of its own in the formal talks, where climate finance is negotiated. Resilient health systems are one of 10 priorities on Türkiye’s voluntary action agenda but, unlike electrification or waste, they have no numerical targets for 2035. “Health is the human face of climate change,” Tedros told ministers. “It belongs in the negotiated text. It should be an explicit eligibility area for climate finance and its share should grow as adaptation finance grows.” New ‘initiative’ launched The headline launch from Health Day came with Türkiye and WHO’s announcement of what is known as the Antalya Initiative for Resilient Health Systems (AIR). It is a voluntary scheme through which countries document what has worked in protecting health from climate shocks, what has not and what it cost, and share those lessons. In short, a shared feedback platform. But no countries announced their participation in the initiative as of Monday night. “We want a successful solution developed in one country to be able to save lives in another,” said Türkiye’s Health Minister Kemal Memişoğlu. “We want to ensure that no country has to waste time reinventing solutions for the same problems.” The initiative is designed to complement WHO’s Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health (ATACH), a network of more than 100 countries that will hold their own summit on Tuesday at the COP31 health pavilion. No funding, staff or list of participating countries has been published. Eighteen health organisations, led by Health Care Without Harm, have asked for the initiative to include a dedicated pillar for health workers. Belém funding framework At COP30 in Belém, Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called the formalising of Belém Health Action Plan a historic shift in the role health plays in climate talks. One year later, it has 40 signatories. Brazil, meanwhile, launched a financing framework for the Belém Health Action Plan, a voluntary list of about 60 non-binding measures now endorsed by 40 countries since it was launched last year. Drawn up with Wellcome and the Rockefeller Foundation, it sets out for each measure which kinds of money could pay for it, from climate funds and development banks to philanthropy and national budgets, along with likely partners and examples of where it has worked. “I wish to make it very clear: this is not a new fund,” Padilha said. “It’s a map to help countries make better use of the mechanisms that already exist.” Much of what the plan covers, such as disease surveillance, early warning systems and training health workers, generates little or no revenue, Padilha said, yet countries are being asked to take on debt to pay for it. COP31 CALL TO ACTION IFRC, as the world’s largest humanitarian network sees the climate crisis as the top global challenge facing humanity and the planet. We need people, places and partnerships to work together to hit climate change head on. Our focus 1 Health and wellbeing. Tackle extreme heat and build climate resilient cities and health systems. We all have a role to play, from governments to cities and local volunteers: to adapt and strengthen health and wellbeing. Our role as the IFRC network IFRC is a Network of 191 Red Cross and Red Crescent National Societies, taking action before, during and after crisis. Together we are scaling up locally led climate action through the Global Climate Resilience Platform and GCRPPooled Fund, supported by IFRC Climate Action Journey, which bridges climate, humanitarian, development, private and innovative finance and support to strengthen community resilience and adapt to climate-related risks. As leaders of the Climate and Environment Charter for Humanitarian Organizations we are committed and reducing our own environmental footprint of our operations and programmes. 2 3 Go local to people and communities, with the quality, quantity and access to climate finance to communities who need it the most. Invest in locally led climate action, local leadership, local ownership driving local solutions. Early action makes early warnings work. Community preparedness and anticipatory action saves lives, protects livelihoods, and minimizes loss and damage, underpinned by effective laws, policies, plans to coordinate and act fast. Investment in people and communities. Timing to get ahead of disasters. 1 Health and wellbeing Heat kills almost half a million people each year.1 Every day the climate crisis is affecting people’s physical and mental health. Global temperature records are being broken month after month and again facing the hottest year ever! Climate change is making heatwaves more extreme. The added influence of El Niño is heightening food insecurity, wildfires and heatwaves - an already silent and deadly killer. As temperatures rise, the scale and nature of climate sensitive health risks is shifting. From vector and water borne diseases, exposing new populations and increasing existing vulnerabilities. It is the most vulnerable communities and people, including displaced persons, who are impacted the most, multiplying existing vulnerabilities due to limited access to safe water, sanitation, food and education. We need to get prepared and scale adaptation efforts. Only 0.5% of multilateral climate funds2 & 4% MDBs3 climate finance goes to health Only 35% of countries reported having health early warning systems for heat related illness.4 Progress: At COP30, global adaptation indicators were adopted, including on health as part of the UAE Framework for Global Climate Resilience. Now progress is needed to align and scale adaptation actions across climate and health. We all have a role to play. National Societies are at the forefront of local action and response to tackle rising heat risk in their communities. Each year we raise the alarm and strengthen preparedness across the world with our Heat Action Day! Our key asks NDCs and NAPs: Integrate and strengthen health and heat action as part of a holistic approach to adaptation action and implementation of national climate plans (NAPs and NDCs). From indicators to action: enhance accessibility of climate finance to strengthen health outcomes and heat action. Enhance shared climate-health outcomes and coordination across government, health systems, local authorities, cities, local actors and communities to scale adaptation action. 1 2 3 4 Beat the heat: invest in multi-sector local action for cities and communities to reduce heat risk. From heat action plans, early warning early action, shock-responsive social protection systems to nature-based solutions to better adapt and reduce risks. sts Peatlands Sustainable Development Goals Transport Youth, education and environment What s new News, stories & speeches Thematic feeds Publications Events Get involved Agenda 2030 Breadcrumb Home News, stories & speeches Press releases As world heads for overshoot of 1.5°C, adaptation is too slow Title As world heads for overshoot of 1.5°C, adaptation is too slow Main image Image Image credit Credit: Timothy K/ unsplash Published on 4 Nov 2026 Body Growth in international public adaptation finance flows are flattening, rising by just US$1 billion between 2023 and 2024 Even if aspiration to triple international public adaptation finance flows to developing countries by 2035 is met, only 20-29 per cent of needs will be covered Beyond finance, governments are strengthening the institutional environment needed to accelerate adaptation implementation Losses and damages are growing in developing countries, but responses and finance remain insufficient Nairobi, 4 November 2026 – With global warming set to exceed 1.5°C, adaptation finance falls far short of needs, implementation is constrained by institutional barriers, and losses and damages are mounting, according to new report from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP). UNEP’s 2026 Adaptation Gap Report: Ready? Not finds that expanded, effective and well-financed adaptation will be crucial to reduce risks, strengthen resilience and support more inclusive development. However, international public adaptation finance flows from developed to developing countries are far below estimated needs of US$305 billion annually by 2035. Even if the COP30 aspiration to triple international public finance flows to developing countries by 2035 is achieved, this would only cover 20-29 per cent of what they need to deal with intensifying climate impacts. “The world is not ready to adapt to current climactic conditions, never mind what overshoot of 1.5°C will bring,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP. “At climate COP31 in Türkiye and beyond, nations must focus on intensifying efforts to achieve the COP30 Global Mutirão aspiration of tripling adaptation finance by 2035 – while understanding that they will need to go even higher to save lives, avoid losses and damages and protect economies.” The state of finance International public adaptation finance flows from developed to developing countries reached US$28.2-31.7 billion in 2024, a US$1 billion increase over the previous year. Flows to least developed countries (LDCs) and small island developing states (SIDS) rose in real terms between 2019 and 2024 but have declined from a 2022 peak, when they should be increasing. Based on an assessment of nationally determined contributions (NDCs), national adaptation plans (NAPs) and model-based estimates, the report provides a central estimate of around US$305 billion in adaptation needs for developing countries annually by 2035. This largely excludes the private sector’s own needs, which could almost double this figure. At COP30, The Global Mutirão decision called for efforts to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035. Depending on whether the tripling is based on current flows or on the Glasgow Climate Pact, international adaptation finance would increase to US$85-120 billion per year by 2035. When adjusted for inflation, the tripling would meet just 20-29 per cent of adaptation finance needs in 2035. More positively, tripling flows to LDCs and SIDS could meet 49-83 per cent of their needs. Positive trends The report does find some positive trends. While growth remains far below the pace required to meet the Glasgow Climate Pact to double finance from 2019 levels to US$40 billion by 2025, the goal could still be met. Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs) are likely to have increased their financing significantly in 2025 – but attaining the goal will depend on whether adaptation flows from bilateral development partners are affected by declining official development assistance. Financial flows between developing countries are also increasing. Contributions through MDBs and direct South-South cooperation rose from US$3.8 billion in 2019 to US$9.6 billion in 2024. Meanwhile, private flows are growing – although they primarily address the private sector’s own adaptation needs or are likely to be paid for

Share: Heat Impacts on Animals and the Environment GHHIN / Kyaw Zay Yar Lin (Myanmar) Related Topics Health Related Publications State of the Climate Update for COP30 Extreme Heat Risk Governance Toolkit and Framework The initiative recognizes that extreme heat has become one of the most deadly, economically and ecologically damaging, and least managed climate-related threats worldwide. Extreme heat claims more than half a million lives every year and resulting in a record 639 billion potential work hours lost in 2024 - equal to USD 1 trillion, or 1% of global GDP. Cities are warming twice as fast as the global average, straining power and transport systems, while heat-driven crop losses are pushing millions into food insecurity. “The World Meteorological Organization State of the Climate Update 2025 showed that 2025 is set to be one of the three warmest years on record. We are seeing an upsurge in extremes - dangerous daytime peaks, with little respite at night. Temperatures of more than 40 °C - sometimes 50 °C - are no longer the exception,” said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo. WMO The new Framework and Toolkit were developed by an international collaboration of national and global experts led jointly by WMO, the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction ( UNDRR ), the Global Heat Health Information Network ( GHHIN ), and Duke University. It responds to the UN Secretary-General's Call to Action on Extreme Heat. It provides practical, evidence-based tools to help decision makers measure and understand the root causes and drivers of heat risk, and strengthen the governance systems needed to manage and adapt to its impacts. The goal: to enable integrated planning, investment, and action by governments, financiers, and stakeholders across sectors and scales. The Framework and Toolkit were unveiled at the high-level event "Extreme Heat Risk Governance: A New Framework and Toolkit for Accelerated Action" at COP30. The event was hosted by Luxembourg with participation from Selwin Hart, Special Adviser and Assistant Secretary-General for Climate Action, Celeste Saulo, Secretary-General of WMO, Kamal Kishore, Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General for Disaster Risk Reduction, and representatives from national governments, development banks, city leaders, and international organizations including the Rockefeller Foundation, EBRD, and the CREWS Initiative. Kamal Kishore, Head of UNDRR, underscored the significance of this milestone: "The broad engagement in shaping this Framework underscores a critical understanding: integrated, multi-sectoral, and multi-scale extreme heat risk governance is no longer optional - it is essential for survival," he said. The toolkit was also promoted at COP30 Health Day on 13 November, which adopted the Belém Health Action Plan recognizing that climate and health are deeply interconnected. It calls for stronger foundations that link research, impact assessment, risk monitoring and early warning. Umbrellas of my city WMO 2021 Calendar Competition / Miroslava Novak Hranjec A global turning point for heat governance By assessing their current governance maturity, countries can identify strengths and gaps, prioritize improvements, and advance toward integrated, systematic heat-risk reduction across short-, medium-, and long-term timeframes. "This Framework provides partners with a clear path and concrete tools to move from fragmented efforts to coordinated systems that save lives and build resilience," said Joy Shumake-Guillemot, co-lead of the Global Heat Health Information Network . "It is practical, adaptable, and informed by science and experience." The Framework emphasizes that heat risk governance is not just about temperature-it's about interdependencies. Extreme heat amplifies risks across sectors, triggering wildfires, poor air quality, power grid failures, transport disruptions, and food supply breakdowns. Managing these cascading impacts demands whole-of-society coordination. Pilots in 2026: Barbados, Senegal, and Cambodia In 2026, the Framework and Toolkit will be piloted in Barbados, Senegal, and Cambodia, with financial support from the Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems (CREWS) initiative, along with other participating countries across regions and governance contexts. These pilots will test practical tools for multi-sector coordination, financing, and anticipatory action-from prevention and preparedness to early warning and response.
